study.title: Sent to Save
study.focus: Did Jesus come to judge the world, or to rescue it?
study.take: This take follows the mission: God's love gives the Son (3:16), the Son's purpose is rescue, not condemnation (3:17), and the believer is not condemned (3:18).
study.closing: If the one with the power to judge came to save, what does that change for you today?

scripture.16: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
scripture.17: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
scripture.18: He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.

verse_questions.16: How far does God's love go, and why does it surprise us?
verse_questions.17: Did the Son come to judge or to save?
verse_questions.18: What happens to the person who believes?

summaries.JFB3.16.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown ask which words of the gospel preachers and missionaries have spoken most often in every age, which have stirred millions of people, and which have brought so many to the feet of Christ. They point to these words about God's love, so simple and yet so majestic, as the ones that kindle self-giving love in cold and selfish hearts.
summaries.MHC3.16.05: Matthew Henry invites us to be amazed that the great and holy God would love a worthless and wicked world with a love of good will, even though he could take no pleasure in what the world had become. He adds that some Jews wrongly thought the Messiah came only in love for their own nation, but Christ says he came in love for the whole world, Gentiles as well as Jews.
summaries.CHR3.16.1.01: Chrysostom hears Jesus saying: do not be shocked that I must be lifted up so that you may be saved. This pleases the Father, who loved you enough to give his Son for slaves, and ungrateful ones at that. Chrysostom notes that a person would hardly do this even for a friend, or readily for a good person. He adds that Jesus speaks briefly here, yet every word carries weight.
summaries.CAL3.16.04: John Calvin says John does not claim that God acted because he saw something in us worth saving. The credit for our rescue goes entirely to God's love. Because God gave his Son so that people would not perish, Calvin concludes that until Christ steps in to rescue the lost, everyone is headed for eternal destruction.
summaries.MHC3.17.01: Matthew Henry says God's design in sending his Son was that the world might be saved through him. He came with salvation in view and in hand, so the offer of life and salvation is sincere and will be made good to everyone who accepts it by faith. God sent him into a guilty, rebellious world, not as a passing visitor like the angels sent before, but as one who lives here.
summaries.AUG3.17-18.1.01: Augustine says that, as far as it is up to the physician, Christ came to heal the sick, and a patient who will not follow the physician's orders destroys himself. Christ is called the Saviour of the world because he came to save the world, not to judge it; the one who refuses to be saved by him is judged by himself.
summaries.CAL3.17.02: John Calvin says John repeats the word world so that no one who keeps to the road of faith will think himself shut out. Calvin reads judge here as condemn, and says this shows the real purpose of Christ's coming: there was no need for him to come to destroy people who were already ruined.
summaries.CHR3.17-18.1.01: Chrysostom says Christ has two comings with different purposes. The first came to forgive, not to examine our actions; the second will be to examine, not to forgive. So of the first Jesus says he came not to condemn the world but to save it, while at the second he will set the sheep on his right hand and the goats on his left.
summaries.MHC3.18.01: Matthew Henry draws out the happiness of believers. Although a person has been a great sinner and stands convicted, once he believes the process is stopped and judgment is held back. This is more than a delay: he is acquitted and discharged, and is not dealt with by the strict justice his sins deserve.
summaries.JFB3.18.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say the believer has passed from death to life the moment he believes. The one who is condemned already is the one who rejects the single way out that God gave his Son to provide, and so chooses to stay condemned.
summaries.CHR3.18.1.01: Chrysostom stresses that the one not judged is the one who believes, not the one who is merely curious or nosy. He adds that people who claim to know God but deny him by their works are not true believers at all, and that Jesus means such a person is not judged in this one respect: for his works he will suffer a severer punishment, but having once believed, he is not punished for unbelief.

labels.jewish_source: A later Jewish writing that Gill cites; not a statement of what people believed in Jesus's day.
